Mortgage rates have pulled back this week as AI investment trade creates volatility in financial markets and Treasury yields fall back below 5%.

It has been revealed that the average rate on 30-year fixed home loans dropped to 7.21% for the week ending Nov. 25, down 7 basis points from 7.28% recorded the week before, according to Freddie Mac. For perspective, rates averaged 6.26% one year ago.

“Mortgage rates moved back down this week, offering modest relief for prospective homebuyers heading into the Thanksgiving holiday,” says Sam Khater, Freddie Mac's chief economist.

According to recent reports, it is all but guaranteed that the Federal Reserve will raise its benchmark rate to curb inflation at the next Federal Open Market Committee meeting on Dec. 8.

The looming hike, combined with the persistence of the war in Iran, pushed the 10-year Treasury yield back toward 4.816% this week, putting mortgage rates on an upward trajectory once again.

The AI investment trade has created volatility in financial markets as investors try to value companies, including the Anthropic IPO, which gave the organization a valuation greater than the value of every home currently listed for sale.

AI-generated wealth is already shaping consumer housing behavior, with San Francisco Bay Area buyers and those in other tech hubs leaning toward higher down payments.

Markets are right now pricing a 97.6% chance of a 25-basis-point increase next month, according to the CME FedWatch tool.

Meanwhile, pending home sales fell to a record low in October, and existing-home sales hit their lowest level since 2010, as the surge in mortgage rates through mid-October took its toll on buyers and sellers.

For buyers who remain active in the market, current conditions offer some meaningful advantages, including less competition from other shoppers, inventory climbing 8.6% year over year, and sellers increasingly willing to negotiate on price.

This week, the median listing price fell 2.4% from a year ago to $400,000, according to the latest Realtor.com weekly housing market update.

"The challenge is that until inflation cools enough to put mortgage rates on a durable downward path, affordability will remain the dominant constraint on the market," says Realtor.com® senior economist Anthony Smith.

Your credit score plays a role when you apply for a mortgage. A credit score will determine whether you qualify for a mortgage and the interest rate you'll receive. The higher the credit score, the lower the interest rate you'll qualify for.

It has been revealed that the credit score you need will vary depending on the type of loan. A score of 620 is a "fair" rating. However, people applying for a Federal Housing Administration loan might be able to get approved with a credit score of 500, which is considered a low score.

Homebuyers with credit scores of 740 or higher are typically considered to be in very good standing and can usually qualify for better rates, which can reduce monthly payments.

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

Recent findings suggest that per the document, that stay will remain in place until CMS publishes its withdrawal notice. Once that has been put forth, the plaintiffs will dismiss their complaints as moot. CMS also agreed not to take further action against agents and brokers during the current open enrollment period.

The moratorium, finalized in September, was a part the agency's broader efforts to root out fraud, waste and abuse on the Affordable Care Act's exchanges.

UPDATED: Nov. 5 at 4:30 p.m. ET.

A federal court has granted a preliminary injunction to two key groups representing insurance brokers over the Trump administration's moratorium on upcoming broker enrollments.

The District Court of Maryland issued the injunction after determining that the National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals and Health Agents for America "have shown that they are likely to succeed on the merits of their claims under the Administrative Procedure Act.".

The court also stated that the organizations made clear they would likely suffer significant harm if the moratorium stays in place.

Sources indicate that NABIP said that the ruling means that it will restart training for newly introduced brokers beginning on Nov. 6.

"Today’s ruling is a significant victory for licensed agents and brokers and the consumers who rely on their expertise," noted NABIP President Mychal Walker in an announcement (PDF). "With Open Enrollment already underway, every day matters.".

"Lifting the moratorium immediately and beginning training tomorrow will help affected professionals get to work assisting individuals and families in finding coverage that fits their needs and budgets," mentioned Walker.

Recent findings suggest that NABIP initially sued on Oct. 15 to challenge the moratorium. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services instituted the moratorium in late September as part of its broader push to combat fraud on the Affordable Care Act's exchanges.

Recent findings suggest that PUBLISHED: Oct. 15 at 5:15 p.m. ET.

The National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals is suing the Trump administration over its moratorium on fresh brokers entering the Affordable Care Act marketplaces.

The organization, the leading trade group for insurance brokers and agents, noted the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services' moratorium impacts close to 19,000 brokers and agents who will be barred from registering ahead of open enrollment.

CMS unveiled the moratorium in late September as part of its ongoing push to root out fraud, waste and abuse. In addition, the agency said it would terminate more than 200 agents and brokers that failed to comply with marketplace standards.

The agency remarked newly introduced brokers and agents were disproportionately responsible for submitting inappropriate enrollments and engaging in behaviors at high risk for fraud.

In an announcement (PDF), NABIP notes that it supports the broader effort to combat fraud, but that CMS' moratorium "threatens the livelihoods of thousands of legitimate, licensed professionals who have not been accused of fraud and limits consumers’ access to professional assistance as they navigate Open Enrollment.".

In a recent development, the organization argues in the lawsuit that the rule instituting the moratorium violates both the Administrative Procedure Act and the Affordable Care Act. The regulation is unlawful as it is "arbitrary, capricious, and unsupported by sufficient evidence," NABIP noted.

The 19,000 agents who would be barred from participating under the rule are part of a critical network of professionals who help consumers find coverage that meets their needs, the organization remarked.

NABIP President Mychal Walker remarked that CMS should look elsewhere in its fraud efforts.

"The existence of fraud is not in dispute. NABIP has raised these concerns with CMS repeatedly and has offered concrete solutions to address them," Walker mentioned in the announcement. "What is in dispute is whether the appropriate response is to exclude thousands of legitimate agents based solely on whether they registered last year, without any individualized evidence about them.".

"There is a better approach: target fraud where it occurs, strengthen the system’s security and hold bad actors accountable while preserving consumers’ access to trusted professionals," Walker continued.

According to recent reports, CMS has taken steps to crack down on brokers as the agency views improper ACA enrollments as a key target in its fight against fraud. CMS officials have repeatedly raised concerns that people are enrolled in ACA plans without their knowledge, or despite being deceased.

Earlier this week, the agency revealed it will purge 189,000 enrollees who are currently listed as enrolled in both ACA intends and other coverage, such as Medicaid or Medicare.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Last year’s sharp U-turn in energy policy came with catastrophic consequences for farmers who were counting on federal assistance for solar power on their land.
  • For those of you newly introduced to the topic, perovskite refers to a new class of relatively inexpensive, easy-to-fabricate solar materials, characterized by a crystalline structure based on the naturally occurring mineral perovskite (see lots more background here).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last year’s sharp U-turn in energy policy came with catastrophic consequences for farmers who were counting on federal assistance for solar power on their land. Still, the pace of innovation in the solar industry never stopped, and farmers may ultimately benefit whenever the policy winds blow in a more positive direction. In one particularly interesting development, the US startup UbiQD has assembled more evidence that its “UbiGro” perovskite-enhanced glass can help hothouse farmers improve their yields while saving water, too.

For those of you newly introduced to the topic, perovskite refers to a new class of relatively inexpensive, easy-to-fabricate solar materials, characterized by a crystalline structure based on the naturally occurring mineral perovskite (see lots more background here).

Sources indicate that raw perovskite is too unstable to function as a solar material on its own, but it can be combined with more durable materials in a solar cell, or in a solar module. Silicon-perovskite combinations are already emerging in the market, for example.

UbiQD developed its UbiGro glass to incorporate sub-microscopic particles of perovskite. Particles of that size are known as “artificial atoms” or quantum dots, as capably explained by scientists at Los Alamos National Laboratory:.

Sources indicate that quantum dots are ultra-small bits of semiconductor matter that can be synthesized with nearly atomic precision via modern methods of colloidal chemistry. Their emission color can be tuned by simply varying their dimensions. Color tunability is combined with high emission efficiencies approaching 100%.

As Los Alamos indicates, quantum dots initially appeared in the LED field of the lighting industry before moving into solar energy applications as a means of ramping up the efficiency of solar cells. By 2016 researchers were experimenting with quantum dots in a perovskite solar cell. The pioneering startup Blue Dot was among those pursuing the perovskite connection.

Activity began to accelerate in 2025 when UbiQD acquired BlueDot. In the meantime, UbiQD had previously hooked up with the US thin film solar manufacturer First Solar to develop quantum dots for solar panels. That project also ramped up in 2025 when UbiQD closed on a $20 million round of Series B funding. According to UbiQD, its enhancements could double the solar conversion efficiency of First Solar’s bifacial solar panels.

In 2025, UbiQD also declared the findings from a study of its UbiGro greenhouse glass. The glass is treated with quantum dots as a means of fine-tuning sunlight to improve crop yields. The study was published by researchers at the University of California – Davis in the journal Materials Today Sustainability under the title, “Spectrally selective quantum dot laminated glass for photonic modulation and climate regulation in greenhouses.”.

— Fresh biomass increased by 37.8%. Plants were nearly 40% heavier, indicating significantly more edible yield.

Industry observers note that — Leaf area was increased by 38.0%. Larger leaf area means higher photosynthetic surface.

— Root length increased by 38.0%. Deeper roots improve water and nutrient uptake, resilience, and shelf life.

Industry observers note that — Light-use efficiency was increased by 41.0%. The plants used sunlight more effectively, with more biomass per photon.

In a recent development, — Nutrient concentrations (N, P, K, Mg, Zn, Cu) were significantly elevated. The crops were more nutritious, with higher levels of essential nutrients.

Industry observers note that — Spectral red:blue ratio increased by 61.0%, with no significant PAR losses. More red light was delivered without sacrificing total usable light levels.

“The findings highlight a promising pathway toward climate-smart greenhouse envelopes that integrate photonics with sustainable food and energy strategies,” the research team concluded.

Industry observers note that in a series of followup trials last Spring, UC-Davis focused on the impact of UbiGro on water consumption by greenhouse-grown lettuce. The results were similarly encouraging.

Recent findings suggest that “Water use efficiency improved by approximately 9%. Lettuce grown under QD glass produced 101 grams of fresh biomass per liter of water compared 93 grams per liter under conventional glass,” UbiQD noted.

“Unlike technologies that require additional energy inputs or changes to irrigation infrastructure, UbiGro glass works passively by optimizing the sunlight already entering the greenhouse while optimizing water use efficiency,” UbiD emphasized in a press statement.

Industry observers note that ubiQD’s VP of Sales and Marketing, Eric Moody, also chipped in his two cents. “It’s an important new area of validation for UbiGro as we continue exploring how our technology can help growers get more from the resources they already use,”said Moody.

According to recent reports, want more details? Check out the study, “Crop Water Use and Evapotranspiration Estimation in Deep Water Culture Hydroponic System under Quantum Dot Glazed Greenhouse,” presented by UC-Davis Ph.D. candidate Mala Parvin at the 2026 American Society of Agricultural and Biological Engineers Annual International Meeting in Indianapolis last July.

First Solar has also been making some moves of its own. The iconic US firm is of particular interest for its focus on CdTe (cadmium-telluride) solar film instead of the silicon formula commonly used around the world. Here in the US, the Department of Energy has been promoting CdTe since the early 1990’s as a domestically sourced alternative to silicon, and it has become particularly popular in utility-scale applications.

First Solar has been embroiled in patent disputes of late, but the dust appeared to be settling last month when the tech giant confirmed a non-exclusive patent licensing agreement with the US firm CubicPV Inc.

Among other, undisclosed terms of the agreement, First Solar will have access to CubicPV patents covering perovskite solar technology in the US. “The license further clears the path for First Solar to continue its development of photovoltaic (PV) devices built with a perovskite semiconductor for the US utility-scale, commercial and industrial, and residential markets, and applies to sales and distribution of those products domestically,” First Solar explains.

Somewhat ironically, if US President Donald Trump were to lend his full support to the domestic solar industry, First Solar would be a feather in his cap. First Solar bills itself as the largest producer of thin film solar in the world, and the largest solar manufacturer of any kind in the Western Hemisphere.

First Solar is also among the solar stakeholders contributing to the President’s oft-stated ambition of bringing more manufacturing back to the US during his time in office. “The Company’s investments include a fresh perovskite development line at its Perrysburg, Ohio, campus that produces small form-factor modules featuring a perovskite semiconductor, allowing First Solar to meet key internal milestones in its perovskite development program, including initial-stage efficiency, stability, and manufacturability objectives,” First Solar notes.

Industry observers note that that’s just for starters. By the middle of next year, First Solar expects to have a pilot line up and running at a facility in Ohio, which will apply the technology to its existing Series 6 solar modules.

In a recent development, in addition, last month First Solar confirmed the start of Phase I of operations at its sixth facility in the US. Located in Gaffney, South Carolina, the latest factory represents another step in First Solar’s onshoring plan for Series 6 production.

“The second phase is forecast to be completed by mid-2027, at which time the approximately $330 million facility is expected to double its annual nameplate capacity to 3.4 gigawatts (GW) and produce the Company’s CuRe technology, while supporting nearly 700 jobs. Approximately 500 of those jobs have already been filled,” First Solar explains.

Industry observers note that for the record, the Gaffney facility expands First Solar’s existing footprint in South Carolina. The manufacturer also operates in Alabama, Louisiana, and Ohio. All together, First Solar anticipates to have a total of 17 gigawatts’ worth of domestic solar module manufacturing under its belt by the end of this year, which is just around the corner.

Photo: Greenhouse lettuce thrives under natural sunlight filtered through specialized glass from the perovskite solar startup UbiQD, while conserving water resources, too (cropped, courtesy of UbiQD).

Ok, Jalopnik admittedly went really hard on enlightening you on everything from immediate upgrades to behind-the-scenes secrets related to "Grand Theft Auto VI" last week. Maybe a little too hard. I promise this one-off discovery was purely out of genuine interest and transportation nerdiness. It's all about Leonida's public transit system.

YouTuber Sonny Evans is not a page I've ever come across in my gaming watches until today, and from what I've seen on his page, he tends to look into the beyond of game play, or simply someone who the wild what-ifs in open world games. The best way to understand his vibes is reading his bio which said: "I walked a bowl of stew across the map in Red Dead Redemption 2 and millions of people actually watched it." My guy. His more recent posted videos include driving a mobility scooter across the entirety of Leonida in GTA 6, following NPCs to see where they go and what they do, and the latest: seeing if GTA 6's public transportation actually works.

Recent findings suggest that sonny inspected the game's public transit ventures, using the in-game maps to navigate from home base to Vice City using the Interstate Loop buses and the metro lines before landing at Vice City airport. He timed the transit moves, mentioning at about 3:28 in the 10-minute video that his commute into Vice City via the Loop bus was 5 hours of game time. This absolutely correlates with the idea that Leonida is a Florida-like state, likely size-wise as well.

Sonny did the same with Vice City's Metro system, using the in-game posted maps and timing boards to see if the trains really did run on time. They did! This unfortunately makes them a little unrealistic, because anyone who has ever taken any form of public transit knows that nothing will be on time. Ever.

According to recent reports, he also found a real, tiny discrepancy. The signs at the stop showing the Northbound and Southbound routes (showing the stops like they do on the Upcoming York City subways) for the trains were identical, which actually makes no sense. This made it a little more challenging for Sonny to figure out which way to go. Luckily, he guessed right and continued on to Vice City's airport.

Sources indicate that this is where the video went a little off of the rails. Sonny discovers a few hidden areas including the underneath room to the luggage carousels. Then there was the speed run of getting past TSA, causing a little chaos, and ended with Sonny (as Jason, the main character) stealing a commercial plane.

So, it looks like if you get stranded somewhere in Leonidas and have no car handy to steal or carjack, you might be able to depend on public transit. The care the creators took in making that entire system work, even if its on-time buses and trains are somewhat unrealistic, is mad impressive. Now to see if someone will do their entire gameplay using just the public transit. I can't be the only person who would watch that.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that despite copious evidence that Elon Musk is little more than a snake oil salesman and carnival barker like P. T. Barnum, the world continues to believe the man is somehow smarter than the rest of us. Few seem to realize his empire is built on nothing more than wildly inflated boasts and  OPM — other people’s money.

Take away the billions Tesla received over the years from other automakers by selling emissions credits and the tech giant likely would have failed early on. Musk recognized the opportunity those emissions credits offered and seized it with both hands. The existence of SpaceX depends almost entirely on the contracts it has secured from the US government.

People (including some here at CleanTechnica) get all weak in the knees when Musk makes his outlandish claims about robotaxis and Cybercabs, but the truth is that, after a decade, we are still waiting for that Model S to leave California, drive across the country, and park itself in a garage in Manhattan without a human driver ever touching the wheel.

Industry observers note that tesla, the car company, has shrunk its model lineup rather than expanding it. The Model S, Model X, and Cybertruck are now out of production, with no replacements in sight. The Roadster 2.0 is a party trick with a very limited potential market. The $25,000 Tesla is completely off the table.

Are the Model Y and Model 3 pretty good cars? Yes, they are. Yet the competition is bringing dozens of latest models to market every month and introducing electric cars to world markets where their lack of exhaust emissions and lower operating costs can be a real benefit to the local population. The fact that Tesla ignores those markets is proof the company is little more than a niche player in the global automotive marketplace.

Musk’s penchant for issuing pie in the sky predictions and boldly going where no one has gone before is now fully underway in the AI madness. In a recent report by the Latest York Times by Grace Kay and Ryan Mac, the pair detail the same Muskian passion for making bold claims and then bullying his employees to make them a reality.

Musk has used his connections to the White House to construct a sprawling (and rapidly expanding) data center — which Musk, with his usual modesty, calls Colossus — in a predominantly minority neighborhood in Memphis, Tennessee. That enterprise has now spread to nearby Mississippi. The local utilities could not possible supply all the electrical power those enormous facilities consume, and so Musk is powering them with portable methane fired generators that spew far more emissions into the air than a modern combined cycle generating station would.

Recent findings suggest that musk cannot wait for environmental reviews and other government restrictions, so he has blanketed the neighborhoods around his data centers with effluvia from those portable generators and used his political clout to suppress opposition to  his plans. AI is too notable to be delayed by such trivial concerns as people’s health or a massive influx of carbon emissions.

Colossus is home — assuming their is such a thing — to Grok, Musk’s AI invention that features the ability to undress virtually anyone for the amusement of pre-pubescent boys. We hear a lot today about Claude, the AI wizard from Anthropic, and ChatGPT from OpenAI, but Grok is hardly ever mentioned in the same breath as those AI tools.

That has placed Musk in a familiar bind. His dreams are far removed from reality, and so he has been forced to rent out computing power (now known simple as “compute”) to his competitors in order to pay the bills. The Times report says he has told employees that “SpaceX is falling behind in AI development, making it more lucrative to rent the company’s computing power out to rivals than use it to improve its own products,” three people told the Times reporters.

In August, Musk temporarily changed the group chat name for his AI team to “Sell compute because we can’t compete,” the Times was told. Then he did what Musk does so well — he tried motivating his people by threatening them. “Anyone wasting GPUs on bullshit while we are failing to compete will be asked to leave immediately, as this constitutes a betrayal of your team.” This type of bullying is typical of Musk, whose motto seems to be, “The beatings will continue until morale improves.”.

Part of the problem is that SpaceX — the nominal owner of Musk’s AI ambitions — is now a public company, after its blockbuster IPO earlier this year. Before, it was a private company with no need to disclose its finances to the outside world. Now, it must justify is lofty valuation with real world results, and the pressure on Musk to justify his bet on AI is intense.

Sources indicate that “SpaceX makes way more money right now renting out compute than from Grok,” said Nicolas Owens, an analyst who covers SpaceX for Morningstar Research, told the New York Times. “Grok is not the premier model in town, so I think it’s more doubtful that they would be able to tip the scale to where serving up A.I. off of their own servers is more lucrative than branching it out to Anthropic.”.

Industry observers note that musk told his engineers in August, “At the end of the day, the only thing that matters for competitiveness is revenue per GPU, not benchmarks. If you can’t pay for your GPUs, then you either go bankrupt or you become a computer rental manufacturer. Move the needle on revenue.”.

Recent findings suggest that and yet, despite such blandishments, the tech giant has shifted resources away from internal AI projects. The Times reports that Mike Nicolls, the president of the AI unit, disbanded the 60 member team behind Grok Imagine, an image and video generation tool that was once a top priority. He told the workers involved the cuts would “better align our structure and resources with critical business priorities.”.

Those priorities now appear to be focused on renting out as much “compute” as possible to competitors such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and anyone else who needs extra computing power to drive the AI revolution forward.

In another attempt to distract the world of finance away from SpaceX’s financial struggles here on Earth, Musk now indicates he has received permission from the Federal Communications Commission to place up to one million data centers into sun-synchronous orbit around the Earth. That means they will be powered by sunlight nearly 24 hours a day, and their cooling needs will be minimized by the low temperatures in space.

SpaceX will build the 98 foot (30 m) long satellites at its Gigasat Factory in Bastrop, Texas, using AI chips manufactured at the 100 million square foot (ten times the size of the Texas Gigafactory) Terafab manufacturing facility in Grimes County, Texas.

On its website, Terafab modestly announces, “We aspire to be a galactic civilization.” To make that happen, first it intends to “Harness all the energy on a planet,” then “Harness all the energy from a star,” and finally “Harness all of the energy in a galaxy.” Some readers may find all this hype and hysteria reminds them of a phrase made popular during Barry Goldwater’s presidential campaign: “In your heart, you know he’s nuts.”.

Sources indicate that in a press release, the FCC remarked it had approved the request to place one million satellites in orbit subject to certain conditions. According to Reuters, SpaceX must begin deployment no ​later than November 2033, deploy 10 percent of the maximum number no later ⁠than November of 2035, and deploy 50 percent by November 2038. Approving the application ​will permit SpaceX “to pioneer emergent technology that advances American leadership in space and artificial intelligence,” the ​FCC said.

Industry observers note that the enormity of this blueprint is illustrated by the fact that, at present, there are only a total of 17,000 satellites orbiting the Earth (not counting the moon). SpaceX originally asked for permission to launch 42,000 Starlink satellites, yet today only 11,000 have been deployed.

Sources indicate that the satellites will be placed in Earth orbit by Starship, a reusable rocket developed by SpaceX. Those rockets are powered by methane, which has led environmental advocates to question the wisdom of the entire data centers in space project. But Elon has demonstrated by his actions with Colossus in Memphis and Mississippi he doesn’t care a flying fig leaf about the harm burning methane can do.

It has been revealed that “Drastically expanding satellites in space has a direct impact on people’s everyday lives as well as the future of our planet,” said Jan Hasselman, senior attorney at Earthjustice. “Agencies that authorize companies looking to space as the next frontier still must operate within the law, and the law requires the FCC to consider all the risks and impacts of these proposals. It is dismaying that the FCC has ignored the law so blatantly and tried to mask the fact with a holiday filing.”.

According to recent reports, the approval by the FCC seems to be in violation of the National Environmental Protection Act (NEPA). Sharp eyed readers will notice that NEPA will be gutted by the proposed Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) that may slip through a lame duck Congress before the end of this year.

“This approval to deploy a million data centers in space without any thought to the impacts on Earth is just a glimpse of what we’ll see during the next two years of Trump,” remarked Sam Sankar, senior vice president at Earthjustice. “This is great example of why Congress should not pass a flawed bill like BAAJA that would lock in terrible projects like this one. Donald Trump is going to do a lot more dirty and lawless deals over the next years, and BAAJA prevents future presidents from reconsidering them.”.

Recent findings suggest that does human civilization need Musk’s Starmind? It seems clear Musk is hellbent on exporting humanity to the moon, Mars, and beyond because he knows for dead solid certain that he and his tech bro cronies will make the Earth uninhabitable in the not too distant future. If you think about what Musk did to Ukraine recently when he unilaterally restricted its access to Starlink, the prospect of him running the world, if not the entire galaxy, should fill you with dread.

Sources indicate that A certifiable lunatic with the power to play God? Be afraid; be very afraid.

This year, for the first time in the event's history, the parade has been postponed from Thanksgiving Day to tomorrow, Saturday, because the forecast called for heavy rain and wind. Industry observers note that okay, I have to apologize to you all. We started this week with a BMW E46 M3, and now, here we are finishing it off with... a BMW E46 M3. With its LS under the hood and a few other challenges, this E46 is also over 20% cheaper than the Monday car.

Say what you will about engine swaps and sullying the purity of so excellent a car as an E46 M3, the reasons behind this particular car's heart transplant may actually make sense. For the moment, however, it has a 5.3-liter LS V8, an engine that likely started life in a pickup or SUV before finding a new home here in this black-over-gray leather M3. It's not an unusual conversion, and the LS fits in the BMW's engine bay without much fuss. According to the ad, the engine drives the original BMW power steering pump, but an A/C compressor wasn't in the cards. That might make the BMW climate controls a bit wonky and make the open top a welcome feature for airflow.

Sources indicate that the ad notes numerous internal and external engine updates, including an aggressive cam, aluminum heads, hardened internals, and a DOD/AFM delete. It runs a special ECU tuned by PCM of Mooresville, North Carolina, a firm that specializes in GM engine tweaking.

Recent findings suggest that other conversion updates include a fresh high-performance clutch ahead of a ZF five-speed manual gearbox and strengthened rear subframe mounts. It all appears tidy and well put together, but the ad lacks details on how the car runs and rides, or even whether the original instruments function.

It has been revealed that as for the car's looks, there are some plusses and minuses. Overall, it looks to be in solid shape with no body damage evident, a seemingly intact top, and the same Style 163M Cross Spoke alloys as we saw on Monday's car. Looking a bit more closely, as you would when considering buying something like this, a few issues stand out. Notably, the clear coat on the top of the rear bumper cap is fading significantly, and the leather on the driver's seat is also starting to give up the ghost. The rest of the upholstery appears to be in decent shape, with only minor scuffing on the passenger seat. The rear seats look like they've never been used at all.

Industry observers note that other things to note: the center console now houses a pair of add-on gauges, canted toward the driver. Those monitor engine coolant temperature and oil pressure. Above that sits a big screen infotainment unit that, hysterically, still has its protective plastic film intact. Per the ad, the car comes with a clean title. It also notes the mileage at 460, but doesn't explain when that count began.

It has been revealed that this being Black Friday, one might expect to find a total door-buster bargain on tap for our consideration and judgment. The thing is, the way this all works is that you decide what's a bargain or not. You're in control. You're the final arbitrator of value. Use this power wisely.

UnitedHealth Group is joining the ranks of insurers that are suing the feds over the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings calculations.

Sources indicate that much like other recent lawsuits, the healthcare giant argues that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services inappropriately used multiple measures in the calculations. Over the summer, a Georgia federal court sided with MA proposal Clover Health, and tossed 20 measures that were used in its 2026 scores.

That legal ruling has been the basis of much of the current round of legal wrangling.

UnitedHealth stated in its complaint that it is bringing the lawsuit to ensure "that their 2027 Star Ratings are calculated in accordance with CMS’s statutory authority and procedural obligations.".

Sources indicate that the star ratings are tied to quality bonus payments for Medicare Advantage aims and listed on the Medicare strategy finder to help individuals identify high-quality coverage. When those payments are lower due to a decline in scores, the insurer may not be as nimble in lowering premiums or enhancing benefits.

Industry observers note that "The Star Ratings carry real consequences," UnitedHealth wrote in the complaint. "A plan’s Star Rating thus directly affects the benefits and healthcare offerings that Medicare beneficiaries receive.".

According to recent reports, UPDATED: Nov. 9 at 2:30 p.m. ET.

Elevance Health is the latest insurer to sue the feds over its performance in the latest round of star ratings for the Medicare Advantage program.

The tech giant sued the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services in District of Columbia federal court on Friday, arguing that the 2027 star ratings calculations violated the Administrative Procedure Act in using 11 measures that it says were adopted unlawfully.

In the lawsuit, the manufacturer said that the harm from including these measures is "concrete and substantial." If they were excluded, it would increase the scores for 12 of its Medicare Advantage contracts and generate $516 million in additional quality bonus payments.

Sources indicate that "Their inclusion therefore does more than violate statutory requirements in the abstract: it depresses Elevance Health’s ratings and reduces the funding available for the following payment year," per the lawsuit. "That funding could support broader supplemental benefits, lower premiums and cost-sharing, and improved care coordination.".

"CMS’s unlawful methodology puts those resources out of reach," the firm stated.

In addition to the financial impacts, Elevance argues that the star ratings scores can also lead to reputational damage that makes it harder for them to compete in the MA market. It also provides prospective enrollees with inaccurate information, the company said.

"Beneficiaries cannot make informed coverage choices when the government’s own comparison tool conveys a distorted assessment of the looks available to them," Elevance noted.

In a recent development, "An artificially depressed rating does not merely place Elevance Health at a competitive disadvantage; it undermines the very comparison the program is supposed to enable," the manufacturer continued. "A rating lowered by unlawful measures presents beneficiaries with a misleading signal of relative quality, rather than a lawful basis for distinguishing among competing aims.".

Industry observers note that UPDATED: Oct. 27 at 2:45 p.m. ET.

CVS Heath's Aetna is joining the ranks of insurers suing over its results in the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings.

The insured filed suit Monday in Georgia's Southern District Court, and argues that 28 measures used by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services to calculate its scores were "unlawfully adopted" and should have been excluded.

The court is the same venue that ruled in favor of Clover Health over the summer, and set aside 20 measures that were used to determine its 2026 scores. That decision, which the feds have appealed, kicked off a broad recalculation of 2026 scores that looked different for insurers outside of Clover, triggering a wave of litigation.

In its lawsuit, Aetna cites the Clover decision in finding that CMS extended beyond its statutory authority in deploying those 20 measures.

According to recent reports, the company stated that calculating its scores using the 28 measures in question will likely cost it $2 billion in 2028 quality bonus payments and rebate retention. Those are funds that the insurer could "apply toward expanding member benefits, reducing premiums and investing in quality improvement.".

Aetna adds that in addition to the monetary loss, having lower scores negatively impacts the company's reputation and its ability to attract potential members.

Industry observers note that "The harm to CVS Health is not exclusively financial; lower ratings carry meaningful reputational harm, which can in turn impact membership," per the lawsuit. "By incorporating unlawful measures into the 2027 Star Ratings calculation, CMS cast CVS Health’s ratings in a poorer light in the eyes of Medicare Advantage consumers relative to peer MAOs, undermining CVS Health’s ability to compete for Medicare beneficiaries through enhanced benefits and the like.".

Aetna did not respond to a request for comment at the time of publication.

It has been revealed that based on an analysis from Stephens, 69% of Aetna's MA members are in plans with four or more stars for 2027, down from 81%. That threshold is the key to securing quality bonus payments.

Aetna's complaint follows others focused on the 2027 scores from Centene and Alignment Healthcare (see those stories below).

Centene has become the latest insurer to sue the federal government over its 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings.

In a lawsuit filed Thursday in Georgia's Southern District Court, the tech giant argues that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services violated the Administrative Procedure Act in determining its latest scores. Centene says that CMS ran afoul of "core statutory safeguards" in deploying 17 measures.

The use of those measures ultimately caused "significant injury" to the organization, according to the complaint. For 2027, 9% of Centene's members are enrolled in plans with at least four stars, which declined from 18% in the prior year.

"In implementing each of the individual Star measures that Centene challenges, CMS violated applicable law and thereby caused Centene to lose out on hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue that Centene could use to strengthen benefits, reduce premiums, and improve health outcomes," the company remarked in the lawsuit.

Recent findings suggest that CMS argues that the court has already sided with a similar argument in its decision in favor of Clover Health earlier this year. In that case, which led to a broad recalculation in scores, the courts set aside 20 measures that were used in determining Clover's star ratings for 2026.

If the 17 measures in question had been excluded in calculating Centene's scores, the firm estimates it would receive $448 million more in quality bonus payments for the 2028 plan year, funds it would deploy to expand benefits, lower premiums and enhance programs like care coordination.

In addition to the financial impact, a drop in star ratings also carries a reputational hit, Centene remarked.

"Beyond the financial impact to the company and its members, depressed ratings also inflict significant reputational damage and diminished membership," the company mentioned in the complaint.

Centene had not returned a request for comment at the time of publication.

Recent findings suggest that PUBLISHED: Oct. 12 at 3 p.m. ET.

Alignment Healthcare sued federal regulators, alleging that its 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings were determined "in flagrant violation" of statute.

In the lawsuit filed Friday in District of Columbia federal court, the insurer says that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services "has completely departed from Congress’s vision of leveraging predictable, valid measures developed with input from providers, intends, and the public" in establishing the methodology for the star ratings.

The manufacturer argues that rather than establish "consistent, stable specifications" for metrics through the traditional rule-making process, the agency instead detailed key measures through a series of "technical notes." This violates the Administrative Procedure Act, per the lawsuit.

The program's star ratings are the critical determinant in quality bonus payments to insurers as well as a tool that aims to make it easier for enrollees and brokers to identify benefits with the highest quality.

"Consistent application of the statutory requirements governing Star Ratings is therefore essential not only to plan payments and competition but also to ensuring that beneficiaries can rely on the Star Ratings as meaningful and comparable measures of plan quality," Alignment remarked in the lawsuit.

It has been revealed that the manufacturer adds that multiple recent court decisions have set aside CMS' star ratings methodology, notably a ruling over the summer in favor of Clover Health that tossed 20 metrics used in the 2026 calculations. A Georgia federal judge determined that 10 measures utilized exceeded CMS' authority, while 10 other measures were promulgated inappropriately.

Industry observers note that CMS recalculated the scores across the board following the ruling, but only set aside the 10 measures that the courts determined were outside the bounds of its regulatory authority. The agency maintained that approach in the 2027 calculations, Alignment argues.

"Congress created the Star Ratings program to allow Medicare Advantage beneficiaries to make informed decisions about initiative enrollment based on clinically validated measures of plan quality that had been subjected to notice and comment," the manufacturer said. "CMS’s contrary approach fails to carry out the vision that Congress set forth by statute.".

The Trump administration has appealed the Clover decision, so that legal case remains ongoing.

It has been revealed that in addition, Alignment argues it suffered reputational and financial damage as a result of its 2027 scores, which plummeted compared to the prior year. Just 25% of its members are in intends with four or more stars for 2027, down from 100% in 2026.

Shares in the manufacturer tumbled following the release of the ratings, though stock prices have rebounded since.

Alignment sued the feds following the Clover decision to secure a recalculation for its scores that aligns with the court's decision, and in a statement to Fierce Healthcare, noted that the lawsuit aligns with that perspective.

It has been revealed that "Our lawsuit seeks to ensure that the Star Ratings program operates as Congress intended and that Alignment is properly compensated for the care we provide," Alignment noted in the statement. "We respect the judicial process and will present our case in court. Because this matter involves pending litigation, we will not comment on the specific legal arguments beyond our filings.".

"Our focus remains on delivering exceptional care, improving health outcomes and advocating for a stable, lawful regulatory framework that supports seniors and strengthens the Medicare Advantage program," the company said.

Catching up was like old times, when we used to have dinner together when I accompanied her on royal tours around the world.".

Northwood added that Markle—who he refers to as "M"—is a wonderful lunch companion because she is "someone with good chat who enjoys a laugh and, crucially, who wants to share the food so that I get to try a bit of everything.".

The pals enjoyed sea bass, French fries, and key lime pie. Northwood noted that "Meghan was happy to go along" with his pescatarian diet.

He also noted that "there is a lot of baby chat" given his recent "solo surrogacy journey," and that he's picked up plenty of "parenting tips" from the mom of two.

Northwood also shared a sweet photo of Markle smiling with his son at her home, posed beside a basket of colorful garden-picked veggies.

Markle, 45, and Harry, 42, are reported to be residing in a property on an estate belonging to their close friends, according to the Daily Mail.

The family plans to stay put for the holidays, marking the children's first British Christmas.

"My wife is very good in the kitchen and so is my mother-in-law, so I'll leave that to them," he mentioned, noting that he hopes turkey and gumbo are on the menu.

The decision to stay in England for the holidays also comes from a desire to keep things simple during a difficult time for Markle's family, as her estranged father, Thomas Markle Sr., has been indicted in Florida on two counts of possession of child pornography.

According to recent reports, "Everything going on with her dad is still weighing heavily on her," a source told People. "She wants the holidays to be as quiet and enjoyable as possible for the family.

"Traveling back and forth would be too much for everyone," the source added.

Industry observers note that A surprising discovery involving vitamin B12 could open fresh possibilities for understanding and potentially treating rare genetic disorders. Researchers found that the vitamin can correct developmental problems in tiny worms carrying a genetic mutation associated with Verheij syndrome, a rare human condition that causes developmental delays, impaired growth, and short stature.

Sources indicate that the findings center on a cellular process called RNA splicing, which helps prepare the genetic instructions cells use to produce proteins. During splicing, unnecessary portions of messenger RNA are removed, and the remaining sections are joined together in the correct order. When this process goes wrong, it can disrupt essential cellular functions and contribute to serious developmental disorders.

Mutations in genes responsible for splicing can cause conditions such as Verheij syndrome. To better understand the effects of these genetic changes, scientists investigated how a related mutation affects growth and metabolism in a laboratory model.

Vitamin B12 Reverses Developmental Defects in Worms.

It has been revealed that the discovery emerged from experiments involving C. elegans, a tiny roundworm commonly used in biological research. The researchers were initially searching for previously unknown genes that influence lifespan when they began examining a mutation in a gene involved in RNA splicing. The same gene is associated with Verheij syndrome in humans.

According to recent reports, worms carrying the mutation developed problems resembling important features of the human disorder. Their growth slowed considerably, and they remained smaller than normal.

Recent findings suggest that to investigate why this happened, the scientists conducted genetic screens and analyzed the worms' metabolism. They discovered that the mutation disrupted specific metabolic pathways that depend on vitamin B12 and are essential for healthy growth and normal cellular activity.

Sources indicate that the researchers then tested whether providing additional vitamin B12 could counteract these changes. Remarkably, the treatment restored the affected metabolic processes to normal and corrected the developmental abnormalities associated with the mutation.

"We were surprised to find that a change in a fundamental process of RNA processing had such a targeted effect on vitamin B12-dependent metabolism," says Jonathan Kölschbach, first author of the study. "Even more exciting was that we were able to largely correct the consequences of this change in the worm model using vitamin B12.".

Could Vitamin B12 Help Treat a Rare Genetic Disorder?

To explore whether their findings might also apply to people, the researchers examined publicly available datasets from human cells. They also worked with Hormos Dafsari, a neuropediatrician at the University Hospital Cologne, to collect blood samples from patients diagnosed with Verheij syndrome.

These investigations uncovered evidence of similar metabolic changes in humans, suggesting that the vitamin B12-related pathways affected in the worms may also play a role in the human disorder.

Although the results are promising, researchers have not yet established whether vitamin B12 supplementation can improve symptoms in people with Verheij syndrome. Additional studies will be necessary to determine whether the benefits observed in worms can be translated into a treatment for patients.

The discovery also raises a broader possibility. Metabolic disruptions may contribute more substantially to diseases caused by faulty RNA splicing than scientists previously recognized. Understanding these connections could help researchers identify fresh therapeutic strategies, potentially extending beyond Verheij syndrome to other rare genetic conditions.

According to recent reports, "Our study is a good example of how basic research on model organisms can provide latest insights into human diseases," claims Adam Antebi, Director at the Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing and lead author of the study. "A fundamental biological question can thus give rise to a new approach that could also become medically relevant in the long term.".

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The hydrogen truck completed the trip, and the project partners demonstrated that a mobile hydrogen supply operation could support a freight vehicle across the mountains.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Loblaw’s Hyundai XCIENT hydrogen fuel-cell truck crossed the Canadian Rockies from Vancouver to Calgary on November 18. The 1,046 km journey attracted enthusiastic coverage as a Canadian heavy-freight milestone. It also illustrated an infrastructure problem that gets much less attention than a successful crossing: the hydrogen had to be brought to the truck.

The Edmonton Region Hydrogen Hub announcement describes three fuelling occasions. The truck started with a fill at HTEC’s Vancouver hydrogen station, then refuelled at Sicamous and Golden from a mobile tube trailer supplied by Powertech. Other project partners arranged the trailer’s transportation and logistics. The tractor hauling the mobile fuel was almost certainly diesel-powered. The public account did not include that support truck’s fuel consumption, emissions or cost.

The hydrogen truck completed the trip, and the project partners demonstrated that a mobile hydrogen supply operation could support a freight vehicle across the mountains. Those are achievements, albeit not novel ones. A fleet operator considering hydrogen needs a more demanding result: dependable places to refuel on repeated journeys, delivered hydrogen prices, vehicle availability, maintenance requirements and the complete cost of the support system. Moving a fuel trailer between planned stops is not the same thing as operating a commercial refuelling corridor.

In a recent development, the three fills also complicate the familiar argument that hydrogen offers heavy trucks a decisive range advantage. Hyundai’s fuel-cell truck has marketed range specifications, but the crossing did not establish that range advantage against battery-electric heavy trucks. Battery trucks had completed demanding Alpine journeys years earlier, and commercial electric freight operations have progressed since then. The comparative distances, energy stops and subsequent operating evidence are important when evaluating what this latest event contributed.

According to recent reports, there is a second question about what happened after the official announcement. In the TFIE Strategy Briefing assessment, I reviewed a bounded sample of news reports and social posts from the week after the journey. The press generally included the mobile refills. The promotional accounts circulating on social media were much more likely to celebrate the distance and mountains while leaving out the operation that supplied the fuel.

That difference matters. A photograph of a truck crossing a mountain pass makes an effective announcement. Refuelling arrangements, energy costs and repeatability are harder to compress into a congratulatory post. As the story travels, a demonstration can start to resemble a commercially proven transport system even when the fundamental business questions remain unanswered.

Industry observers note that loblaw also operates battery-electric freight vehicles. Those trucks are making commercial deliveries and accumulating service kilometres rather than appearing in a single supported trial. Comparing the deployment record within the same firm with the attention lavished on its hydrogen journey is a useful way to test how publicity can distort perceptions of technological maturity.

In a recent development, the earlier TFIE analysis, Hydrogen Has Narrative Density. Electrification Has Deployment Density, identified that mismatch across several energy and transport markets. The Loblaw event shows the mechanism: an attractive milestone generates attention while the surrounding operating system receives less attention, and routine electric deployment barely enters the story.

The project partners have mentioned operational results will follow. The decisive questions concern delivered fuel, support logistics and recurring freight service, rather than whether a fuel-cell truck can make one successful trip with dedicated logistical support. Fleet investment requires operating evidence, not publicity counts.

The full TFIE Strategy Briefing quantifies the media-versus-social disclosure gap, compares the driving legs with an earlier battery-electric mountain crossing, and sets the demonstration against Loblaw’s existing electric-fleet deployment. A free subscription opens the complete assessment and its two analytical graphics.

The broader narrative-density assessment traces the same gap between announcements and deployments across energy sectors.

CMS issues Medicare Advantage proposals aimed at boosting competition" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Trump administration has proposed a slew of changes to Medicare Advantage and Part D designed to "revitalize care" in these markets.

According to recent reports, for one, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services said late Friday that it will update application and network adequacy requirements to make it easier for fresh entrants. The agency proposed to require organizations to demonstrate network adequacy during their first year in operation, rather than during the application process.

This shift would eliminate a significant barrier for upcoming entrants, driving greater competition in the market.

CMS has also proposed combining three specialty areas in behavioral health—clinical psychology, clinical social work and outpatient behavioral health—into one specialty group for the purposes of network adequacy. The changes will give intends greater flexibility in building out behavioral health networks.

CMS will also make adjustments that seek to boost competition for special needs prepares.

In addition, the agency mentioned it will make adjustments to the star ratings program, focusing its ratings on 15 measures. The proposed measure set would emphasize "clinical outcomes and patient experience while retaining select process measures in high-priority areas where performance remains low.".

CMS is also aiming to patch the calculation methodology that will "raise the bar for achieving high ratings," and thus quality bonus payments.

"People with Medicare should be able to choose coverage based on what matters most to them—quality, affordability and access," said CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, M.D., in the announcement. "These proposals are about creating a Medicare Advantage marketplace that rewards better care and better value while empowering beneficiaries with the options and knowledge they need to make informed decisions about their health.".

It has been revealed that the proposed rule also includes provisions that align with Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy's Make America Healthy Again agenda by setting a "healthy food" standard that MA plans should follow for supplemental benefits.

The goal, CMS remarked, is to ensure that Medicare dollars are spent on food benefits that align with MAHA.

"Medicare food benefits should pay for nutritious food that helps people improve their health and manage chronic disease," Kennedy said in the announcement. "This proposal would require those benefits to meet the Dietary Guidelines for Americans while preserving access to foods and nutritional products that providers recommend for patients’ specific medical needs.".

"Under President Trump, we are putting prevention at the center of health care and demanding more from every Medicare dollar," Kennedy said.

Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1246 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that an eight-year study of children in Finland has revealed a surprising connection between screen time and brain function.
  • The findings suggest that the amount of time children spend in front of screens may be less vital than how they use that time.
  • According to recent reports, the discovery comes amid growing concerns about insufficient physical activity among teenagers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that an eight-year study of children in Finland has revealed a surprising connection between screen time and brain function. Researchers found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the widespread assumption that screen time is necessarily harmful to developing brains.

The findings suggest that the amount of time children spend in front of screens may be less vital than how they use that time. Activities that encourage learning, creativity, and problem-solving could be particularly valuable. Researchers emphasize that the goal should not be to eliminate screen time, but to balance it with physical activity and mentally stimulating experiences.

According to recent reports, the discovery comes amid growing concerns about insufficient physical activity among teenagers. A sedentary lifestyle has been linked to poorer academic performance, while regular exercise is known to support brain function, particularly in adults. However, scientists still have much to learn about how physical activity, sitting, and screen use during childhood influence thinking abilities later in adolescence.

These questions are especially crucial because childhood and adolescence are critical periods of brain development. Changes in attention, memory, and learning during these years can have lasting consequences, potentially influencing educational opportunities and career paths well into adulthood.

To investigate these relationships, Finnish researchers examined how screen time, physical activity, and sedentary behavior from childhood through adolescence were associated with cognitive performance in teenagers. They also explored whether the connections differed between boys and girls and whether the intensity of physical activity made a difference.

More Screen Time Linked to Better Thinking Skills.

One of the study's most unexpected findings was that greater screen time throughout childhood was associated with better cognitive processing in adolescence.

Recent findings suggest that cognitive processing refers to the mental abilities people use to take in information, pay attention, remember details, learn fresh things, and solve problems. These abilities play an notable role in school performance and everyday decision-making.

The findings challenge the idea that all screen time should be viewed as harmful. However, the researchers caution that the relationship may depend on what children are actually doing while using digital devices. Watching videos, playing games that require strategic thinking, and engaging in educational activities may involve very different levels of mental effort.

Industry observers note that "The findings suggest that screen time can support children's and adolescents' cognitive processing. Presumably, the essential point here is what kind of things they do in their screen time. Teachers and parents should encourage children to use devices and screens in such ways that promote active thinking, problem-solving, creativity, and learning," states Doctoral Researcher Petri Jalanko from the University of Jyväskylä.

"We should not regard screen time solely as harmful but seek balance between physical activity and screen time that promotes active thinking," Jalanko summarizes.

Exercise Affects Boys' and Girls' Brains Differently.

The researchers also uncovered a more complicated picture of how physical activity relates to thinking and memory.

Among girls, spending more time engaged in light-intensity physical activity since childhood was associated with better working memory during adolescence. For boys, greater participation in guided physical activity over the same period was linked to stronger working memory.

Working memory is the brain's ability to temporarily hold and use information. It allows someone to remember instructions while completing a task, keep track of numbers during mental calculations, or follow a conversation while processing upcoming information.

Sources indicate that light-intensity physical activity generally includes relatively gentle movements that do not substantially increase breathing or heart rate. Guided physical activity refers to exercise carried out with some form of instruction or supervision, such as organized sports or structured exercise sessions.

The differences between boys and girls suggest that the relationship between exercise and brain health may depend on more than simply how much a person moves. The type of activity, how it is organized, and the individual's sex could all play a role.

Another Surprising Finding About Physical Activity.

The study produced another counterintuitive result. Teenagers who reported spending less time in unsupervised physical activity tended to perform better on measures of cognitive processing.

Yet when researchers used wearable sensors to objectively measure movement and heart rate, they found no association between overall physical activity or sedentary time and cognitive performance.

Industry observers note that one possible explanation is that wearable devices measure movement without revealing what a person is actually doing. For example, a sensor may record periods of sitting or physical activity, but it cannot determine whether someone is solving a difficult problem, studying, participating in an organized activity, or simply resting.

This distinction could help explain why questionnaire responses revealed relationships that were not apparent in the sensor measurements.

"Our study indicates that the connections of physical activity and sedentary behavior to cognitive processing are complex and depend on the sex, the type and assessment method of physical activity and sedentary time. Moreover, boys and girls may benefit from different types of physical activity in view of brain health," Jalanko adds.

"However, we need more intervention studies to find out causal relations and sex differences in this respect. Moreover, it is key to examine more specifically the effects of the intensity of physical activity on changes taking place in cognitive processing.".

What the Eight-Year Study Revealed.

The findings come from an eight-year follow-up conducted as part of the PANIC study, a long-running Finnish research project investigating children's physical activity and nutrition.

Sources indicate that the current analysis included 260 participants, consisting of 124 girls and 136 boys. Their average age at the adolescent assessment was 15.8 years.

It has been revealed that researchers collected information about physical activity and sedentary behavior using both questionnaires and wearable devices that combined heart rate monitoring with movement measurements. This approach allowed them to compare participants' reported activities with data collected by sensors.

According to recent reports, to evaluate cognitive abilities, the researchers used the CogState test battery, a collection of computerized assessments designed to measure aspects of mental performance. The tests examined learning, attention, and working memory.

Importantly, the findings show associations rather than cause and effect. They do not establish that increasing screen time will improve a child's thinking abilities or that reducing certain types of exercise will produce cognitive benefits. Intervention studies, in which researchers deliberately change participants' activities and measure the results, are needed to determine whether these relationships are causal.

Sources indicate that nevertheless, the results offer an vital perspective on the continuing debate over children's screen use. Rather than treating all time spent with digital devices as equally harmful, the researchers suggest paying closer attention to whether those activities encourage active thinking and learning.

The research also highlights the importance of considering different forms of physical activity rather than focusing exclusively on the total amount of exercise children receive.

Together, the findings suggest that supporting healthy brain development may require a more nuanced approach, one that combines physical activity with opportunities for learning, creativity, and mental engagement, including those that take place on screens.

The study was published in the scientific journal Pediatric Exercise Science.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

London, UK — GRIDSERVE, the UK’s most-used electric vehicle (EV) charging network, has secured a £420 million financing package, marking a significant milestone in the company’s financial development and providing a strengthened funding platform for its next phase of growth.

One of the largest financing packages of its kind in the EV charging sector, the deal comprises a £240 million loan to refinance existing debt, a £165 million capital expenditure facility to fund future investment in the network and a £15 million revolving credit facility to support working capital and liquidity.

Structured as green senior debt under GRIDSERVE’s Green Finance Framework, the financing was anchored by the National Wealth Fund, Crédit Agricole CIB, NatWest and Rabobank as cornerstone lenders, each acting as Mandated Lead Arranger alongside MUFG, with MUFG also acting as Sole Financial Advisor. The package strengthens the tech giant’s long-term funding position, providing greater financial flexibility and dedicated capital to support its ongoing investment in critical UK EV charging infrastructure.

The refinancing also reflects the significant financial progress GRIDSERVE has made under CEO Daniel Kunkel. In 2025, the organization reported positive EBITDA for the first time in its history, following a renewed focus on disciplined investment, utilisation-led growth and capital efficiency. The new financing structure builds on this progress, providing a robust foundation for sustainable growth and continued investment in the business.

Since opening its first EV charging station in Braintree in 2020, GRIDSERVE has established itself as a leading force in the transition to electric mobility. Its nationwide network now supports an average of 350,000 charging sessions every month across more than 200 locations. GRIDSERVE also remains the only UK charging operator to have invested in a dedicated interoperability testing facility, helping to underpin its 99% availability record and ensure that upcoming electric vehicle models, regardless of manufacturer, can charge seamlessly across its network.

Alongside continued investment in its existing network, the upcoming capital expenditure facility will support GRIDSERVE’s next phase of expansion, including the development of ultra-rapid EV charging provision beyond the motorway network.

Sources indicate that daniel Kunkel, CEO of GRIDSERVE, said: “Securing this refinancing package is a significant milestone for GRIDSERVE and reflects the progress we have made over the last year. We have demonstrated that our network can grow sustainably, supported by a disciplined approach to investment, utilisation and capital efficiency.

“The strength of this financing package, and the confidence shown in us by our lending partners, puts GRIDSERVE in a strong position for the future. It reinforces our long-term commitment to the UK and gives us the funding platform to continue investing in the infrastructure needed to decarbonise road transport. We look forward to building on this momentum as we enter the next phase of our growth.”.

Oliver Holbourn, National Wealth Fund CEO, remarked: “Drivers need confidence that reliable charging will be available where they need it before making the switch to electric. By lending alongside commercial banks, the National Wealth Fund is supporting GRIDSERVE’s continued investment in its network, including prepares to expand ultra-rapid charging beyond motorways. This is about backing the infrastructure that makes cleaner transport a practical choice for more people.”.

Priya Veerapen, Managing Director, Infracapital, said, “GRIDSERVE has made significant progress since our investment in 2022, and this £420 million refinancing marks an key next step in its growth. Alongside TPG, we have invested more than £300 million in the business, reflecting our conviction in the long-term need for high-quality EV charging infrastructure and the important role GRIDSERVE can play in delivering it across the UK.”.

Recent findings suggest that jamie Gilbert, Business Unit Partner at TPG Rise Climate, stated: “The strength of this refinancing reflects the quality of GRIDSERVE’s business and the progress the company has made in establishing itself as a leader in UK EV charging. It also underscores the importance of continued investment in the infrastructure needed to support the UK’s transition to electric mobility.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that when we first drove the Mustang Shelby GT500KR back in 2020, we called it a preposterous 760-horsepower daily drivable monster. The funny thing is, this currently listed monster on Bring a Trailer has been modified to produce an even more preposterous 900 horsepower.

Sources indicate that shelby American produced a limited-run of factory-made special-edition GT500KRs as part of Shelby American's 60th-anniversary celebration. Those cars got a 60th-anniversary badge and were dubbed King of the Road. — hence the KR tacked on to the model name.

In a recent development, the GT500KR received a number of modifications to differentiate it from the standard GT500, including the supercharger and intercooler, upgraded adjustable springs and revised sway bars, and big Brembo brakes – specifically, six- and four-piston (front and rear, respectively) stoppers with ventilated rotors. Shelby offers the body kit and tuning to owners of 2020-22 GT500KRs for $54,495. But it was only open to 60 cars for the 2020 model year (a total of 225 over a three-year period), making this a very rare Mustang indeed.

Sources indicate that we don't know what this GT500KR will cost when the gavel finally drops on this auction, but the original pricer was $127,895 for the direct-from-Shelby version. So the final price likely won't be cheap — especially for a Mustang.

Thinking about this another way, though, it's a deeply modified, 900-horsepower machine that can likely keep up with expensive supercars from the likes of Porsche or Ferrari. And Shelby American didn't just bolt on parts. They claim that they worked closely with Whipple to develop a 3.8-liter capacity supercharger with a larger throttle body, cold air intake, and a revised pulley system, as well as a multi-core intercooler. Shelby also made certain the car would pass emissions across the U.S.

Shelby American also worked directly with Ford on the carbon fiber hood – the side vents suck heat from the exhaust manifold to prevent heat soak from robbing the V8 of power. Forged 6061-T6 aluminum wheels were specifically developed for this version of the Shelby GT500KR, too, and buyers could get them in either brushed silver or gloss black. The black looks sweet, but I think this car would look equally special with silver rims. As befits a street racer, this Mustang gets Recaro front buckets in red-and-black leather, with grippy Alcantara side bolsters.

There aren't very many comps for the GT500KR, so setting expectations for the price is a bit tough. A few older models from the 1968 run have sold for well over $200,000, as have a few low-mileage versions of the most modern KR. A 592-mile example of the 2022 KR was bid recently to $153,000, but it didn't sell. Maybe the KR's sibling, the Code Red, could lend a bit of perspective.

Recent findings suggest that in 2022, Shelby also brought back the twin-turbo Code Red with 1,300 horsepower and made just 30 examples. That car cost $209,995 when it was newly introduced, and it wasn't street legal, so you'd need a very big wallet and track access to enjoy it. To make that much power, Shelby swapped the supercharger for twin turbochargers. It also gave the car a unique, dual-fuel feed so it can run on racing octane as well as E85. A Code Red was also up for auction on Bring a Trailer recently, and it was bid up to $282,500 — but that didn't meet the seller's reserve.

Recent findings suggest that you want a 2020 GT500KR with 900 horsepower to drive, though, not to be parked in a collection like that 226-mile Code Red most likely has been. And you can't street drive the Code Red. This car hits the sweet spot for insane power that's still usable, and no matter what price it goes for, this GT500KR should be driven. With 21,000 miles already on the clock, that's the sort of treatment it deserves.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
Photon pharmacy marketplace integrated with ChatGPT for clinicians" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Photon, a prescription infrastructure firm, is now available as a plugin for ChatGPT to streamline prescribing for clinicians within a tool they already use.

According to recent reports, the option is available to eligible U.S. licensed clinicians using ChatGPT for Clinicians (free for verified clinicians) or ChatGPT for Healthcare. Just as clinicians must accept OpenAI’s BAA before sharing protected patient information, they must accept Photon’s BAA to maintain HIPAA compliance when using Photon in ChatGPT. Controlled substances are not supported. The feature is free for clinicians through Dec. 31, 2026.

The patient experience remains the same through Photon. What is fresh is where the clinician can write a prescription. Clinicians with a Photon account can draft, review and send prescriptions without leaving ChatGPT. They just need to add the Photon plugin into ChatGPT, and then they can draft prescriptions. A patient will get a text to Photon’s prescription marketplace outside of ChatGPT. Patients can compare prices and request to change a pharmacy as needed.

Industry observers note that “AI is moving from note-taking and reference into treatment workflows. Clinicians are already using ChatGPT to understand treatment options. Once they’ve decided what to prescribe, they should be able to act on that decision in the same conversation,” Otto Sipe, co-founder and CEO, wrote to Fierce Healthcare in an emailed comment. “Photon provides the infrastructure behind that step.”.

In the new interface, clinicians begin a prompt with the name of the patient and medication. Photon uses authorized patient information and treatment context shared with ChatGPT to help prepare a prescription for a clinician’s review. They can also add new patient details during the process. Once saved in Photon, that patient can be found by name for future prescriptions.

Industry observers note that from there, clinicians review the prescribing details, including the dosing, instructions and quantity. Clinicians can ask about dosing options in the chat. Patient records are saved in Photon, and draft prescriptions are checked against the patient’s recorded allergies and medications. Finally, clinicians review and authorize the prescription to be sent, remaining responsible for the treatment. Clinicians can check a prescription’s status in ChatGPT.
